bug_description.normalized: GetBuildId() walks PT_NOTE entries using a caller-supplied buffer and length. The staged 12-byte witness is exactly one little-endian `ElfW(Nhdr)` with `n_namesz = 4`, `n_descsz = 0xFFFFFFFB`, and `n_type = NT_GNU_BUILD_ID`. Vulnerable code computes `desc_start = 16`, then wraps the aligned total `size` back to 12 when it adds the huge aligned descriptor span. The corruption guard only checks `size < sizeof(*nhdr)` and `note + size > last`, so it accepts this impossible note even though `desc_start` already lies past the 12-byte buffer and `size < desc_start`. Because `n_type` still selects the build-id path, `note_name = note + sizeof(*nhdr)` becomes exactly the end of the heap-backed testcase buffer and `memcmp(note_name, "GNU\0", 4)` performs the reproduced AddressSanitizer heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 4. The fix adds the missing wraparound and bounds checks on `desc_start`, `size < desc_start`, and `size > last - note`.

tainted_value_origin.code: const ElfW(Nhdr)* const nhdr = reinterpret_cast<const ElfW(Nhdr)*>(note);
tainted_value_origin.description: Reinterprets the first 12 attacker bytes as an ELF note header, yielding `n_namesz = 4`, `n_descsz = 0xFFFFFFFB`, and `n_type = 3 (NT_GNU_BUILD_ID)`.

source.description: Creates the PT_NOTE scan window over the attacker buffer; `note` points to the testcase bytes and `last = note + pt_note->p_filesz` marks the 12-byte upper bound later used by the corruption checks.
source.value_from: `info->dlpi_addr` is the fuzz buffer pointer and `pt_note->p_filesz` is its 12-byte length from the `data,size` pair wrapped by the harness.

root_cause.code: if (nhdr->n_namesz >= static_cast<ElfW(Word)>(-align) || nhdr->n_descsz >= static_cast<ElfW(Word)>(-align) || size < sizeof(*nhdr) || note + size > last) {
root_cause.description: The vulnerable corruption guard fails to reject the wrapped geometry because `size` has wrapped back to 12. It never checks that `desc_start` already lies past the buffer or that `size < desc_start`, which is exactly what the fix adds.

sink.description: With `note_name == last`, `memcmp(note_name, "GNU\0", 4)` reads 4 bytes starting at the end of the 12-byte heap testcase buffer and triggers the observed AddressSanitizer heap-buffer-overflow read.

fine_trace.note: Constructs the PT_NOTE scan window over the attacker buffer. For the staged witness, `note` points to byte 0 of the 12-byte testcase and `last = note + pt_note->p_filesz` points to byte 12.

fine_trace.code: const ElfW(Nhdr)* const nhdr = reinterpret_cast<const ElfW(Nhdr)*>(note);
fine_trace.note: Materializes the first 12 attacker bytes as one ELF note header: `n_namesz = 4`, `n_descsz = 0xFFFFFFFB`, and `n_type = 3 (NT_GNU_BUILD_ID)`.
The truncated-header guard is false because the scan window is exactly 12 bytes long and `sizeof(*nhdr)` is also 12, so parsing continues instead of rejecting the note.
Using `n_namesz = 4` and `align = 4`, the aligned descriptor offset becomes 16. In this 12-byte note, the descriptor would start 4 bytes past `last`.

The aligned descriptor span is `0xFFFFFFFC`; adding that to `desc_start = 16` wraps the unsigned `ElfW(Word)` total back to 12. The computed entry size now aliases the original header length instead of the real enormous note extent.

fine_trace.code: if (nhdr->n_namesz >= static_cast<ElfW(Word)>(-align) || nhdr->n_descsz >= static_cast<ElfW(Word)>(-align) || size < sizeof(*nhdr) || note + size > last) {
fine_trace.note: This corruption check still treats the forged note as valid: `n_namesz` and `n_descsz` stay below the `-align` threshold, `size < sizeof(*nhdr)` is false because both are 12, and `note + size > last` is false because `note + 12 == last`. The vulnerable code never checks that `desc_start` already exceeds the buffer or that `size < desc_start` after wrap-around.
Because the forged header advertises `NT_GNU_BUILD_ID`, execution enters the build-id-specific path instead of skipping this note.

depends_on.via: nhdr->n_namesz >= static_cast<ElfW(Word)>(-align) || nhdr->n_descsz >= static_cast<ElfW(Word)>(-align) || size < sizeof(*nhdr) || note + size > last

fine_trace.code: const char* const note_name = note + sizeof(*nhdr);
fine_trace.note: Inside the build-id branch, `note_name` becomes `note + 12`, which is exactly `last`. No note-name bytes exist inside the 12-byte buffer.

The left conjunct is true because `n_namesz = 4`, so `memcmp(note_name, "GNU\0", 4)` reads 4 bytes starting from `note_name == last`. AddressSanitizer reports the resulting heap-buffer-overflow READ at this line.

depends_on.via: nhdr->n_namesz >= static_cast<ElfW(Word)>(-align) || nhdr->n_descsz >= static_cast<ElfW(Word)>(-align) || size < sizeof(*nhdr) || note + size > last

coarse_trace.summary: GetBuildId parses the attacker-wrapped PT_NOTE buffer, computes a wrapped note size that slips past the corruption guard, then compares a 4-byte GNU name starting at the end of the 12-byte heap input.

parser_admitted.description: The harness wraps the testcase as one PT_NOTE program header, so execution immediately enters GetBuildId's `while (note < last)` note parser on the attacker buffer.

patch_analysis.patch_description: The fix keeps the existing `n_namesz`/`n_descsz` prechecks but strengthens the corruption guard to reject wrapped `desc_start`, wrapped `size`, and any entry length larger than the remaining `[note, last)` span.

key_changes.change: Replaces `size < sizeof(*nhdr) || note + size > last` with `desc_start < sizeof(*nhdr) || size < desc_start || size > last - note`, which rejects this witness's `desc_start = 16`, `size = 12` wraparound case.
Adds a minimized regression testcase for the overflowing PT_NOTE header.

format.name: Single forged PT_NOTE ElfW(Nhdr) header
format.contract: The witness is exactly 12 bytes: `04 00 00 00 fb ff ff ff 03 00 00 00`. Interpreted as one little-endian `ElfW(Nhdr)`, those bytes set `n_namesz = 4`, `n_descsz = 0xFFFFFFFB`, and `n_type = 3 (NT_GNU_BUILD_ID)`. No note-name or descriptor bytes follow the header, so the vulnerable parser reaches `memcmp(note + 12, "GNU\0", 4)` on the saved crash path.
